decks.title: Ecosystem — Part 1: Structure and function
goals: Define an ecosystem and give examples of its types
Describe the biotic and abiotic components and stratification
Describe the structure and functions of a pond ecosystem

slides.heading: Ecosystem
slides.body_md: Part 1 — an ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact among themselves and with their physical surroundings.

visual.alt: Flow showing biotic and abiotic components forming an ecosystem

slides.narration: An ecosystem can be as small as a pond or as large as a forest or a sea. Many ecologists regard the entire biosphere as a global ecosystem made of many local ones. Because the global ecosystem is too big to study at once, we divide it into smaller units.

slides.heading: Types of ecosystems
slides.body_md: Ecosystems are broadly **terrestrial** or **aquatic**, and some are **man-made**.

visual.alt: Table of terrestrial, aquatic and man-made ecosystems with examples

slides.narration: Forests, grasslands and deserts are terrestrial ecosystems. Ponds, lakes, wetlands, rivers and estuaries are aquatic. Crop fields and an aquarium are ecosystems made by people. All of them work on the same basic principles.

slides.heading: Structure: biotic and abiotic
slides.body_md: In an ecosystem, **biotic** and **abiotic** components interact and function as a unit. The interaction produces a **physical structure** characteristic of each type of ecosystem. Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species gives its **species composition**.

rows: Water, soil, dissolved inorganic and organic substances, sunlight, temperature

visual.alt: Table of ecosystem components with examples

slides.narration: The living part of an ecosystem includes producers, consumers and decomposers. The non-living part includes water, soil, minerals, light and temperature. The two parts are linked: plants take minerals from the soil, and decomposers return them.

slides.heading: Vertical stratification
slides.body_md: The vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels is called **stratification**. In a forest, **trees** occupy the top vertical strata or layer, **shrubs** the second, and **herbs and grasses** the bottom layers.

slides.narration: Walk into a forest and look up. The tallest trees form a canopy, shrubs grow beneath them, and herbs and grasses cover the ground. Each layer receives a different amount of light and supports different animals. This layering is called stratification.

slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the plants closest to the ground.

slides.heading: A pond ecosystem
slides.body_md: A pond is a shallow water body in which all the basic components of an ecosystem are well exhibited.

rows: Water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances; rich soil deposit at the bottom
Solar input, cycle of temperature, day length and other climatic conditions
Phytoplankton, some algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants
Fungi, bacteria and flagellates, abundant at the bottom

visual.alt: Table of the components of a pond ecosystem

slides.narration: In a pond, tiny floating phytoplankton and larger plants are the producers. Zooplankton and fish are consumers. Fungi, bacteria and flagellates at the bottom decompose dead matter. Sunlight, temperature and day length control how fast the pond works.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting a pond
slides.body_md: A student lists what she found in a pond sample. Sort each into abiotic, producer, consumer or decomposer.
bullets: Dissolved phosphate and the mud at the bottom → **abiotic**.
Phytoplankton and a submerged water plant → **producers** (autotrophs).
Zooplankton and a small fish → **consumers**.
Bacteria and fungi in the bottom sediment → **decomposers**.

visual.alt: Worked table sorting pond items into four categories

slides.narration: Ask whether each item is alive, and if so, how it gets food. Minerals and mud are abiotic. Organisms that make food by photosynthesis are producers. Those that eat others are consumers. And bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter are decomposers.

slides.heading: Functions of a pond
slides.body_md: A pond performs all the functions of any ecosystem, and of the biosphere as a whole.

nodes.label: Autotrophs convert inorganic material into organic material using the sun’s radiant energy
Dead organic matter is decomposed and mineralised, releasing minerals for reuse
Energy moves one way to higher trophic levels and is lost as heat

visual.alt: Flow of the four functions of a pond ecosystem

slides.narration: Producers capture sunlight and make organic matter. Consumers eat the producers. Decomposers break down dead matter and return minerals for reuse. Energy, however, flows only one way, towards higher trophic levels, and is lost as heat along the way.

slides.heading: Quick check: pond producers
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the pond ecosystem.
slides.narration: Quick check. Do minerals and energy behave in the same way?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: four components of function
slides.body_md: The four important components of ecosystem function are productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Match each to an event in a pond.
bullets: Phytoplankton make new organic matter in sunlight → **productivity**.
Bacteria break down a dead fish into simpler substances → **decomposition**.
A fish eats zooplankton, gaining part of its energy → **energy flow**.
Phosphate released from the dead fish is taken up again by algae → **nutrient cycling**.

visual.alt: Worked table matching pond events to the four ecosystem functions

slides.narration: Each pond event illustrates one function. Making organic matter is productivity. Breaking down dead matter is decomposition. Passing food energy up a chain is energy flow. And re-using released minerals is nutrient cycling.

slides.heading: Quick check: decomposers
slides.body_md: Where are decomposers especially abundant in a pond?
slides.narration: Quick check. Where does dead matter collect?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ecosystem: functional unit where organisms interact among themselves and with the physical environment; biosphere is the global ecosystem.
Types: terrestrial, aquatic, man-made.
Structure: biotic and abiotic components; species composition; stratification (trees, shrubs, herbs and grasses).
Pond: phytoplankton and plants (producers), zooplankton and fish (consumers), bacteria, fungi and flagellates (decomposers).
Functions: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling.

visual.alt: Summary table of forest strata

slides.narration: To recap: an ecosystem is a unit of living and non-living parts working together. Its structure includes species composition and stratification. And every ecosystem, from a pond to the biosphere, carries out productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define **ecosystem** and **stratification** precisely.
Name the **components of a pond** with examples.
List the **four functions** of an ecosystem.
Say that energy flow is **unidirectional** while minerals are **recycled**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Define ecosystem and stratification. Name the parts of a pond with examples. List the four functions. And remember that energy flows one way while minerals are recycled.

decks.title: Ecosystem — Part 2: Productivity and decomposition
goals: Define primary and secondary productivity, GPP and NPP
Calculate NPP from GPP and respiration
Describe the steps of decomposition and the factors that affect it

slides.heading: Productivity and decomposition
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how much organic matter an ecosystem makes, and how dead matter is broken down.

visual.alt: Flow from sunlight to producers, consumers, detritus and minerals

slides.narration: A constant input of solar energy is the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain. Producers use it to make organic matter, and decomposers later break down whatever dies, returning minerals to the soil.

slides.heading: Primary production and productivity
slides.body_md: **Primary production** is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis, expressed as weight (g per square metre) or energy (kcal per square metre). The **rate** of biomass production is **productivity**.

rows: Rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis
Part of GPP used by plants themselves
GPP − R: biomass available to consumers
Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers

visual.alt: Table of productivity terms and meanings

slides.narration: Productivity is expressed per unit area per unit time, so ecosystems can be compared. Plants use a considerable part of what they make for their own respiration. Only what remains, the net primary productivity, is available to herbivores and decomposers.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from GPP to NPP
slides.body_md: A crop field has a GPP of 2400 kcal per square metre per year, and the plants use 900 kcal per square metre per year in respiration. Find the NPP and the percentage of GPP used in respiration.
bullets: Respiration share $= \dfrac{900}{2400} \times 100 = 37.5$ percent.
NPP is what herbivores and decomposers can use.

headers: kcal per square metre per year

visual.alt: Worked table: NPP equals 1500

slides.narration: Subtract respiration from gross productivity to get net productivity: fifteen hundred kilocalories per square metre per year. The plants used a little over a third of what they made just to stay alive.

slides.heading: Quick check: NPP
slides.body_md: Calculate NPP from GPP and respiration.
slides.narration: Quick check. Subtract respiration from GPP.

slides.heading: What controls productivity?
slides.body_md: Primary productivity depends on the **plant species** in an area, **environmental factors**, **availability of nutrients** and the **photosynthetic capacity** of plants, so it varies between ecosystems.

rows: Annual NPP of the whole biosphere
Share of Earth’s surface covered by oceans

visual.alt: Table of biosphere productivity figures

slides.narration: Although oceans cover about seventy percent of the Earth’s surface, they produce less than a third of the biosphere’s net primary production. The rest comes from land. Nutrients and light are often in short supply in the open ocean.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: land versus ocean
slides.body_md: Of about 170 billion tons of NPP made each year, the oceans make 55 billion tons. How much is made on land, and what percentage comes from the oceans?
bullets: Land $= 170 - 55 = 115$ billion tons.
Ocean share $= \dfrac{55}{170} \times 100 \approx 32.4$ percent.
So about 70 percent of the surface gives only about a third of the production.

visual.alt: Worked table: land 115, ocean 55 billion tons

slides.narration: Subtracting gives one hundred and fifteen billion tons on land. The oceans contribute about thirty-two percent of the total even though they cover most of the planet. This tells us ocean productivity per square metre is low.

slides.heading: Decomposition
slides.body_md: Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like **carbon dioxide, water and nutrients**. The raw material is **detritus**: dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead remains of animals, including fecal matter.

nodes.label: Fragmentation: detritivores (earthworm) break detritus into small particles
Leaching: water-soluble nutrients go down into the soil and precipitate as unavailable salts
Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances
Humification: dark, amorphous humus forms; resistant, decomposes very slowly
Mineralisation: humus degraded by microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients

visual.alt: Flow of the steps of decomposition

slides.narration: An earthworm is often called the farmer’s friend because it breaks detritus into small pieces and loosens the soil. Fragmentation, leaching and catabolism go on at the same time. Humus is colloidal and acts as a reservoir of nutrients, which are released slowly by mineralisation.

slides.heading: Quick check: decomposition steps
slides.body_md: Which step of decomposition is carried out by earthworms?
slides.narration: Quick check. Earthworms break things into pieces.

slides.heading: Factors affecting decomposition
slides.body_md: Decomposition is largely an **oxygen-requiring** process. Its rate is controlled by the **chemical composition of detritus** and by **climate**.

rows: Rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances such as sugars

visual.alt: Table of factors that speed up or slow down decomposition

slides.narration: Leaves rich in sugars and nitrogen rot quickly, while woody material rich in lignin, or insect remains rich in chitin, rot slowly. Warm, moist conditions favour decomposers. Cold or oxygen-poor conditions slow decomposition, so organic matter builds up.

slides.heading: Quick check: factors
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about decomposition.
slides.narration: Quick check. What do lignin and chitin do to the rate?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Primary production: biomass made per unit area by plants; productivity is its rate (g or kcal per square metre per year).
NPP = GPP − R; secondary productivity is made by consumers.
Biosphere NPP about 170 billion tons a year; oceans only 55 billion tons.
Decomposition: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation.
Faster with nitrogen and sugars, warmth, moisture and oxygen; slower with lignin, chitin, cold and anaerobiosis.

visual.alt: Summary table of key relations

slides.narration: To recap: productivity measures how fast an ecosystem makes organic matter, and net primary productivity is what is left after the plants’ respiration. Decomposition turns detritus into minerals through five steps, and its rate depends on the detritus and the climate.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **NPP = GPP − R** and give **units**.
Name the **steps of decomposition in order** and the organisms involved.
Explain the **effect of lignin, chitin, temperature and moisture**.
Define **humus** and its role.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the relation between gross and net productivity with units. Name the decomposition steps in order. Explain the factors that change the rate. And define humus.

goals: Trace the flow of energy through grazing and detritus food chains
Construct and interpret pyramids of number, biomass and energy and state their limitations

slides.heading: Energy flow and ecological pyramids
slides.body_md: Part 3 — where the energy goes, and how we picture it.

visual.alt: Flow of energy from the sun through producers to herbivores and carnivores

slides.narration: Except for deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth. Of the incident solar radiation, less than half is photosynthetically active radiation, and plants capture only two to ten percent of it. Yet this small amount sustains the entire living world.

slides.heading: Unidirectional flow of energy
slides.body_md: Energy flows **one way**: from the sun to producers and then to consumers. Ecosystems are not exempt from the **second law of thermodynamics**; they need a constant supply of energy to make the molecules they require and counteract the tendency towards disorder. At each step energy is lost as **heat**.

slides.narration: Green plants are producers. All animals depend on plants, directly or indirectly. Herbivores are primary consumers, and the carnivores that eat them are secondary consumers. At every step much of the energy is used in respiration and lost as heat, so it cannot be recycled.

slides.heading: Grazing and detritus food chains
slides.body_md: The **grazing food chain (GFC)** starts with living plants, for example grass → goat → man. The **detritus food chain (DFC)** starts with **dead organic matter** and is made of decomposers, mainly **fungi and bacteria** (saprotrophs), which secrete digestive enzymes and absorb the products.

rows: Detritus food chain carries a much larger fraction of energy

visual.alt: Table comparing the main energy route in aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems

slides.narration: In water, most energy passes through grazing food chains. On land, a much larger share flows through detritus food chains. The two are linked: animals of the detritus chain may be eaten by animals of the grazing chain. Such interconnected chains form a food web.

slides.heading: Trophic levels and standing crop
slides.body_md: Organisms occupy a place in the ecosystem according to their source of nutrition, called a **trophic level**: producers first, herbivores (primary consumers) second, carnivores (secondary consumers) third. Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time, the **standing crop**, measured as **biomass** or **number per unit area**.

visual.alt: Table of trophic levels with examples

slides.narration: The number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is limited by the ten percent law: only about ten percent of the energy at one level passes on to the next. After a few levels too little energy remains to support another population.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the 10 percent law
slides.body_md: Producers in a grassland fix 50000 J of energy. Using the 10 percent law, how much energy reaches the primary, secondary and tertiary consumers?
bullets: Primary consumers $= 50000 \times 0.1 = 5000$ J.
Secondary consumers $= 5000 \times 0.1 = 500$ J.
Tertiary consumers $= 500 \times 0.1 = 50$ J.
The rest is lost mainly as heat in respiration at each level.

visual.alt: Worked table: 50000, 5000, 500, 50 joules

slides.narration: Multiply by one-tenth at each step. Fifty thousand joules at the producers becomes five thousand, then five hundred, then only fifty at the tertiary consumers. That is why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels.

slides.heading: Quick check: 10 percent law
slides.body_md: Apply the 10 percent law to a food chain.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide by ten at each step.

slides.heading: Ecological pyramids
slides.body_md: The relationship between trophic levels can be shown as a pyramid of **number**, **biomass** or **energy**. The base is the producers and the apex the top consumers. Pyramids of number and biomass are usually upright, but the **pyramid of biomass in the sea is inverted**, as the biomass of fishes (and zooplankton) far exceeds that of phytoplankton. The **pyramid of energy is always upright**.

sections.heading: 1. Ecosystem: structure and function
sections.body_md:
An **ecosystem** is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact among themselves and with their surrounding physical environment. Its size ranges from a small pond to a large forest or a sea; the entire **biosphere** is regarded as a global ecosystem.

**Types:** **terrestrial** (forest, grassland, desert) and **aquatic** (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary); **man-made** ecosystems include crop fields and an aquarium.

**Structure.** Biotic and abiotic components interact and function as a unit, giving a physical structure characteristic of each ecosystem. Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species gives the **species composition**. **Stratification** is the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels: in a forest, **trees** occupy the top layer, **shrubs** the second, and **herbs and grasses** the bottom layers.

**Pond ecosystem.**
- Abiotic: water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances, and the rich soil deposit at the bottom. Solar input, the cycle of temperature, day length and other climatic conditions regulate the rate of function.
- Autotrophs: phytoplankton, some algae, and floating, submerged and marginal plants.
- Consumers: zooplankton, and free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms.
- Decomposers: fungi, bacteria and flagellates, especially abundant at the bottom.

**Functions** (pond and biosphere alike): conversion of inorganic into organic material by autotrophs using the sun’s radiant energy; consumption of autotrophs by heterotrophs; decomposition and mineralisation of dead organic matter, releasing minerals for reuse; unidirectional movement of energy towards higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as heat.

**Four important components of ecosystem function:** productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

key_terms.definition_md: A functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact among themselves and with the physical environment.
Vertical distribution of different species at different levels in an ecosystem.
The identity and number of plant and animal species in an ecosystem.

sections.heading: 2. Productivity
sections.body_md:
A constant input of solar energy is the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain.

- **Primary production:** the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis; expressed as weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²).
- **Productivity:** the **rate** of biomass production, expressed in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹, so that different ecosystems can be compared.
- **Gross primary productivity (GPP):** the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. A considerable amount of GPP is used by plants in **respiration (R)**.
- **Net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP − R:** the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers).
- **Secondary productivity:** the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting an area, environmental factors, availability of nutrients and the photosynthetic capacity of plants. The annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about **170 billion tons** (dry weight) of organic matter. Although oceans occupy about **70 percent** of the surface, their productivity is only **55 billion tons**; the rest is on land.

key_terms.definition_md: The rate at which plants produce biomass per unit area.
Gross primary productivity: rate of production of organic matter in photosynthesis.
Net primary productivity: GPP minus respiration losses; available to heterotrophs.
The rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

sections.heading: 3. Decomposition
sections.body_md:
Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients. The raw material, **detritus**, is dead plant remains such as leaves, bark and flowers, and dead remains of animals, including fecal matter.

**Steps:**
1. **Fragmentation:** detritivores (e.g. earthworm) break detritus into smaller particles.
2. **Leaching:** water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
3. **Catabolism:** bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances.
4. **Humification:** accumulation of a dark coloured amorphous substance, **humus**, that is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes at an extremely slow rate. Being colloidal, it serves as a reservoir of nutrients.
5. **Mineralisation:** humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients.

Fragmentation, leaching and catabolism operate simultaneously on the detritus.

**Factors.** Decomposition is largely an **oxygen-requiring** process. Its rate is controlled by the **chemical composition of detritus** and **climatic factors**. It is **slower** if detritus is rich in **lignin and chitin**, and **quicker** if it is rich in **nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars**. **Warm and moist** conditions favour it; **low temperature** and **anaerobiosis** inhibit it, resulting in a build-up of organic material.

key_terms.definition_md: Dead plant and animal remains, including fecal matter, the raw material for decomposition.
An animal, such as an earthworm, that breaks detritus into smaller particles.
Dark, amorphous, colloidal organic matter that is resistant to decay and stores nutrients.
Release of inorganic nutrients from humus by microbes.

sections.heading: 4. Energy flow
sections.body_md:
Except for the deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystem, the **sun** is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth. Of the incident solar radiation, **less than 50 percent** is photosynthetically active radiation (**PAR**); plants capture only **2–10 percent of PAR**, and this small amount sustains the entire living world.

There is a **unidirectional flow of energy** from the sun to producers and then to consumers. Ecosystems are not exempt from the **second law of thermodynamics**: they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise the molecules they require, to counteract the universal tendency towards increasing disorderliness.

- **Producers:** green plants. **Consumers:** all animals depend on plants directly or indirectly. **Primary consumers** (herbivores: insects, birds and mammals on land; molluscs in water); **secondary consumers** (carnivores) and so on.
- **Grazing food chain (GFC):** grass → goat → man.
- **Detritus food chain (DFC):** begins with dead organic matter; made of decomposers (heterotrophs, mainly fungi and bacteria — **saprotrophs**) that secrete digestive enzymes and absorb the products.
- In an **aquatic** ecosystem the GFC is the major conduit of energy flow; in a **terrestrial** ecosystem a much larger fraction of energy flows through the DFC. The DFC may be connected with the GFC at some levels; the natural interconnection of food chains is a **food web**.
- **Trophic levels:** producers (first), herbivores (second), carnivores (third). Each level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time, the **standing crop**, measured as biomass or number per unit area.
- The number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is restricted because transfer of energy follows the **10 percent law**: only about 10 percent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower one.

A food chain that begins with dead organic matter and decomposers.
The mass of living material, or number of organisms, at a trophic level at a particular time.
Only about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next.

sections.heading: 5. Ecological pyramids
sections.body_md:
The relationship between producers and consumers can be shown as a **pyramid** of **number**, **biomass** or **energy**, with the producers at the base and top consumers at the apex.

- **Pyramid of number:** usually upright (many grass plants, fewer herbivores, very few top carnivores); inverted when one large tree supports many insects.
- **Pyramid of biomass:** usually upright on land; **inverted in the sea**, because the biomass of fishes (and zooplankton) far exceeds that of phytoplankton at any time.
- **Pyramid of energy:** **always upright**, never inverted, because when energy flows from one trophic level to the next some energy is always lost as heat.

**Limitations:** pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain, which almost never exists in nature, and do not accommodate a food web; and saprophytes are given no place in them, even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.

A pyramid in which a higher trophic level is larger than the one below it.

questions.stem_md: What is an ecosystem? Describe its structure, using a pond as an example, and explain the functions that every ecosystem performs.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Definition.** An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact among themselves and with their surrounding physical environment. It may be as small as a pond or as large as a forest; the whole biosphere is a global ecosystem. Ecosystems may be terrestrial, aquatic or man-made.

**Structure.** Biotic and abiotic components interact to give a structure characteristic of each ecosystem, described by its species composition and stratification; in a forest, trees, shrubs and herbs occupy different layers. In a pond, the abiotic part is water with dissolved substances and the soil at the bottom, regulated by sunlight, temperature and day length. Producers are phytoplankton, algae and floating, submerged and marginal plants; consumers are zooplankton and free-swimming and bottom-dwelling animals; decomposers are fungi, bacteria and flagellates at the bottom.

**Functions.** Autotrophs convert inorganic into organic material using the sun’s radiant energy; heterotrophs consume the autotrophs; dead organic matter is decomposed and mineralised so that minerals are reused; and energy moves one way towards higher trophic levels and is lost as heat. These correspond to productivity, decomposition, nutrient cycling and energy flow.

questions.solution_md: Definition, structure with pond, functions.

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps by which detritus is decomposed in soil.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Fragmentation:** detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles.
2. **Leaching:** water-soluble nutrients move down into the soil and are precipitated as unavailable salts.
3. **Catabolism:** bacterial and fungal **enzymes** degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances.
4. **Humification** forms **humus**, which decomposes very slowly.
5. **Mineralisation:** microbes degrade humus, releasing **inorganic nutrients**.

Conifer needles and woody litter are rich in **lignin**, which decomposes slowly, whereas soft leaves rich in **nitrogen and sugars** break down quickly. So litter **accumulates** in the cold forest.

questions.stem_md: Explain the process of decomposition, naming each step, and discuss the factors that control its rate.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Decomposition.** Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water and nutrients. The raw material is detritus: dead plant remains such as leaves, bark and flowers, and dead animal remains including fecal matter.

**Steps.** In fragmentation, detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles. In leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and are precipitated as unavailable salts. In catabolism, bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. These three steps occur simultaneously. Humification then produces humus, a dark, amorphous, colloidal substance that resists microbial action, decomposes extremely slowly and acts as a reservoir of nutrients. Finally, in mineralisation, some microbes degrade humus and release inorganic nutrients.

**Factors.** Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process. Its rate depends on the chemical composition of detritus: it is slow when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quick when it is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances such as sugars. Climate also matters: warm and moist conditions favour decomposition, while low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, so organic material builds up.

questions.solution_md: Steps and factors.

questions.stem_md: Explain primary and secondary productivity, gross and net primary productivity, and the factors on which primary productivity depends. Use biosphere figures to compare land and oceans.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Primary production** is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis, expressed as weight (g per square metre) or energy (kcal per square metre). Its rate is **primary productivity**, expressed in g or kcal per square metre per year, so that ecosystems can be compared.

**GPP and NPP.** Gross primary productivity is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. Plants use a considerable part of it in respiration (R). What remains, NPP = GPP − R, is available for consumption by heterotrophs, both herbivores and decomposers. **Secondary productivity** is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

**Factors.** Primary productivity depends on the plant species in an area, environmental factors, the availability of nutrients and the photosynthetic capacity of the plants, so it varies between ecosystems.

**Land and oceans.** The biosphere’s annual NPP is about 170 billion tons (dry weight). Although oceans cover about 70 percent of the surface, they produce only about 55 billion tons; about 115 billion tons come from land, so productivity per unit area is much lower in the oceans.

answer.model_answer_md: The **grazing food chain** begins with **living green plants** eaten by herbivores, e.g. **grass → goat → man**. The **detritus food chain** begins with **dead organic matter**; its decomposers, mainly **fungi and bacteria (saprotrophs)**, secrete enzymes and absorb the products. In **aquatic** ecosystems the **grazing chain** is the main conduit of energy; on **land** a much larger fraction flows through the **detritus chain**. The two are linked in **food webs**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the flow of energy in an ecosystem. Explain why it is unidirectional, distinguish grazing and detritus food chains, and explain how the 10 percent law limits the number of trophic levels.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Source.** Except for deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy. Less than 50 percent of incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), and plants capture only 2–10 percent of PAR; this small amount sustains the living world.

**One-way flow.** Energy flows from the sun to producers and then to consumers. Ecosystems obey the second law of thermodynamics: they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise molecules and counteract the tendency towards disorder, and at every transfer much energy is lost as heat, so it cannot be recycled.

**Food chains.** Green plants are producers; herbivores are primary consumers and carnivores secondary consumers. The grazing food chain starts with living plants (grass → goat → man). The detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter and is made of decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria, which are saprotrophs. In water the grazing chain is the main route of energy; on land much more energy flows through the detritus chain. Linked chains form food webs.

**Trophic levels.** Each trophic level has a standing crop. Only about 10 percent of the energy at one level passes to the next, so after four or five levels too little energy remains to support another population.

questions.solution_md: Source, one-way flow, chains, 10 percent law.

marking_scheme.step: GFC and DFC with land and water

questions.stem_md: What are ecological pyramids? Describe pyramids of number, biomass and energy, explaining with examples when each can be inverted, and state their limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Ecological pyramids** show the relationship between trophic levels in terms of number, biomass or energy. The base is always the producers and the apex the top consumers.

**Pyramid of number.** In a grassland it is upright: very many grass plants support fewer herbivores, still fewer carnivores and very few top carnivores. It is inverted when one large tree supports many insects.

**Pyramid of biomass.** On land it is usually upright. In the sea it is generally inverted, because at any time the biomass of fishes and zooplankton far exceeds that of the phytoplankton, which are small and reproduce rapidly.

**Pyramid of energy.** It is always upright and can never be inverted, because when energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat; each level therefore has less energy than the one below it, roughly 10 percent passing on.

**Limitations.** Pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain and do not accommodate a food web; and saprophytes are given no place in them, although they play a vital role in the ecosystem.

questions.solution_md: Definition; three pyramids with inversions; limitations.

marking_scheme.step: Pyramid of biomass with inversion in the sea
Pyramid of energy always upright with reason
